newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO ministers battle to the end over labour rights.
newsitem.headline: WTO ministers battle to the end over labour rights.

text.p: Trade ministers were debating down to the wire on Thursday over the vexed question of whether the World Trade Organisation (WTO) should be involved in improving standards for workers, a senior official said.
"The position is still fluid. I can't say whether there will be agreement tonight or tomorrow," said Indian Commerce Secretary Tejendra Khanna.
The United States has been adamant that the issue be included in the final declaration of the WTO's first ministerial conference, effectively the WTO agenda, when it ends on Friday.

Washington, supported by some European nations, including France, insists that voters' concerns over 250 million child labourers, mostly in the developing world, and sweatshop conditions must be tackled to maintain public support for global free trade.
India was one of the countries which began the conference, which operates by consensus, on Monday saying it did not want to see any mention of the subject in the final declaration.
Such countries, mostly Asian, said they saw the U.S. push as an attempt to use the WTO trade disputes proceedures to undermine the competitive advantage of low-cost labour in developing nations.
They said the issue should remain the sole concern of the International Labour Organisation (ILO), which was set up to deal with labour standards.
However, India, along with the United States, was part of a small group of ministers which thrashed out language on Thursday to present to the 128 nations attending the conference.
But Khanna, the top official in India's commerce ministry, said some developing nations continued to insist into the evening that there be no mention of labour rights in the final declaration.
"A lot of developing countries continue to say they prefer the issue not be reflected in the final declaration. They feel there is no relationship between trade and labour standards per se," he said.

"Some say that even if this is the case, it's better to get it endorsed and so mandated by the ministers that these issues are not related and therefore there should not be further reference to them at the WTO," Khanna said.
"People are saying if we can find satisfactory language that can express that definitively, perhaps we will be able to go along," he said.
India itself had reserved its position, he added.

Conference sources said the draft language did refer to the ILO as "the competent body" to set and promote good labour standards and that the ILO and the WTO would "continue their existing collaboration" on the issue.

"We reject the use of labour standards for protectionist purposes and agree that the comparative advantage of countries, particularly developing countries, must be in no way put into question," the draft said, according to the sources. Asian diplomats said the language went a long way towards meeting their concerns, but it was still not clear whether all developing nations would agree to its inclusion in the final declaration.
"There are some people who still believe deeply there should be no mention of labour standards and it's not clear whether this language will satisfy them," said one.
